questions.question: Two paragraph elements are stacked vertically in normal document flow. Paragraph 1 has `margin-bottom: 35px;`. Paragraph 2 has `margin-top: 20px;`. Under standard CSS margin collapsing rules, what is the EXACT vertical pixel distance between the borders of the two paragraphs?
options: 55px (35px + 20px)
35px
15px (35px - 20px)
20px
questions.explanation: In CSS, adjacent vertical margins between block-level elements in normal document flow undergo 'Margin Collapsing': they do not add together ($35 + 20 \ne 55$). why_wrong.3: 20px is the smaller margin; the cascade selects the maximum value (35px).

questions.topic: CSS Box Model, Flexbox & Responsive Layouts
questions.question: Name the four concentric components of the CSS Box Model from inside out.
questions.answer: 1. Content, 2. Padding, 3. Border, 4. Margin.
questions.explanation: The W3C CSS Box Model consists of four concentric rectangular layers from inside out: 1) Content (text/media dimensions defined by width and height); 2) Padding (transparent clearance area around content inside the border); 3) Border (visible boundary stroke wrapping padding and content); and 4) Margin (transparent buffer clearing external surrounding elements). (W3C CSS Box Model Level 3).

questions.answer: When two adjacent vertical margins meet in normal document flow, they collapse into a single margin equal to the larger of the two values, rather than adding together.
questions.explanation: Applies strictly to vertical margins in block layout; horizontal margins never collapse.

questions.topic: CSS Box Model, Flexbox & Responsive Layouts
questions.question: Contrast `display: none` with `visibility: hidden`.
questions.answer:
`display: none` removes the element completely from document layout (no space allocated).
`visibility: hidden` hides the element visually, but preserves its exact width, height, and blank space in the layout.
questions.explanation: In CSS layout, 'display: none' removes the element entirely from the document flow as if it did not exist, causing surrounding elements to collapse into its space. In contrast, 'visibility: hidden' hides the element visually while preserving its exact physical dimensions and layout footprint on the page. (MDN Web Docs; W3C CSS Display).

questions.question: What does `position: fixed` do, and what is a common use case?
questions.answer: It removes the element from document flow and positions it relative to the browser viewport. The element remains in the exact same screen position even when the user scrolls the page. Common use case: persistent top navigation bars or floating action buttons.
questions.explanation: Frequently used for sticky UI headers and sidebars.

questions.question: Calculate the actual rendered width of EACH card under default `content-box`, and explain why the 3 cards failed to fit side-by-side in the 900px container.
options: Each card is 300px; they failed because CSS prohibits 3 cards in one row
Each card rendered width is 344px (300px width + 40px padding + 4px border); three cards require 1032px, which exceeds the 900px container by 132px, forcing line wrapping
Each card rendered width is 260px; they failed because the container was too wide

questions.question: Why did the page heading disappear underneath the navbar, and what CSS rule fixes Bug 1?

questions.topic: CSS Selectors, Specificity & Typography
questions.question: Why is 'External CSS' (using `<link rel="stylesheet" href="styles.css">`) considered the undisputed software engineering best practice over 'Inline CSS' for commercial multi-page websites?
options: Because external CSS is the only method that can render red text

Because external CSS cleanly separates presentation from HTML structure, allows thousands of pages to share a unified visual theme, and enables browsers to cache the stylesheet once to drastically accelerate page loading speeds
Because inline styles are strictly prohibited by the CPU processor hardware
Because external CSS automatically translates HTML code into C programming language
questions.explanation: External stylesheets adhere to the Separation of Concerns principle. Storing styles in a dedicated `.css` file allows hundreds of HTML pages to link to a single stylesheet (simplifying site-wide redesigns) and allows client browsers to cache the file after the first request, saving bandwidth and boosting performance. Inline styles violate DRY (Don't Repeat Yourself) and severely degrade maintainability.

why_wrong.0: Inline, internal, and external CSS can all render red text identically.
why_wrong.2: CPUs do not execute CSS directly; web browser rendering engines parse CSS.
why_wrong.3: CSS is a style sheet language; it has nothing to do with compiling C code.

questions.topic: CSS Selectors, Specificity & Typography
options: Red, because `alert` is listed first in the HTML `class="warning alert"` attribute
Blue, because `.warning` is declared later in the CSS stylesheet source order than `.alert`
Purple, because the browser blends red and blue together
Black, because conflicting class names cancel each other out
questions.explanation: Both selectors (`.alert` and `.warning`) have identical specificity: 1 class selector (0, 0, 1, 0). The order of class names inside the HTML attribute (`class="warning alert"`) has ZERO effect on CSS priority. Under the CSS Cascade, when two competing rules have equal specificity, the rule that appears LATER in the CSS source code wins. Because `.warning { color: blue; }` is written after `.alert { color: red; }`, the color is blue.

why_wrong.0: The order of class names in the HTML `class` attribute does not influence CSS cascade priority.
why_wrong.2: Browsers do not mix colors; one CSS rule completely overrides the other.
why_wrong.3: Conflicting rules do not cancel out to black; the cascade resolves the conflict deterministically.

questions.topic: CSS Selectors, Specificity & Typography
questions.question: What is the primary advantage of using `rem` (Root EM) units instead of `em` units for sizing typography on a responsive web page?
options: `rem` units make text permanently un-editable by hackers
`rem` scales relative to the root `<html>` font size (default 16px) and avoids the compounding multiplication problem of `em` inside deeply nested elements
`rem` units only work on Apple Mac computers
`em` units can only be used for image widths, not font sizes

why_wrong.0: CSS measurement units have zero relation to cybersecurity or hacker prevention.
why_wrong.2: `rem` is an open W3C standard supported across all modern web browsers on all operating systems.
why_wrong.3: `em` is widely used for typography, padding, and margins.

questions.question: Why did `.btn-danger` fail to change the button color to red?
options: Because the browser does not support the color red on Tuesdays
Because `#confirm-drop` is an ID selector with a specificity of (0,1,0,0) (score 100), which completely overrules the class selector `.btn-danger` with a specificity of only (0,0,1,0) (score 10)
Because button elements cannot have background colors in CSS
Because the word 'danger' is blocked by university proxy filters
questions.explanation: Under W3C CSS Specificity rules, an ID selector (`#confirm-drop`) carries a specificity weight of 100, which completely overpowers a class selector (`.btn-danger`, weight 10), regardless of source code order. why_wrong.3: Network proxies filter HTTP packets; they do not edit CSS class names.

125px

questions.topic: HTML Forms, Inputs, Tables & Media Elements
questions.question:
A form contains two non-editable fields:
`Field A: <input type="text" name="matric" value="2024/001" readonly>`
`Field B: <input type="text" name="role" value="Student" disabled>`
When the user clicks the submit button, what data is sent to the backend server?

`matric=2024/001` will be submitted, but `role` will NOT be submitted at all
`role=Student` will be submitted, but `matric` will NOT be submitted
Both `matric` and `role` will be submitted normally
questions.explanation: This is a classic web examiner trap. The `readonly` attribute prevents the user from altering the text, but the field's `name` and `value` ARE included in form submission. why_wrong.2: `disabled` fields are omitted from form payloads; `role` is not sent.

questions.question: What is the primary technical function of the `<!DOCTYPE html>` declaration at the beginning of an HTML document?

It instructs the web browser's rendering engine to parse and render the document in standard HTML5 mode rather than legacy 'quirks mode'

questions.question: In modern HTML5 web standards, what is the exact difference between the `<strong>` element and the `<b>` element?
options: `<b>` renders text in red color, while `<strong>` renders text in blue color
`<strong>` conveys semantic importance and urgency (which assistive screen readers emphasize with a changed tone of voice), whereas `<b>` is purely presentational styling with zero semantic meaning
`<strong>` can only be used inside tables, while `<b>` can only be used inside headings
There is no difference whatsoever; both are identical and `<b>` is preferred in HTML5
questions.explanation: In HTML5, `<strong>` represents strong semantic importance, seriousness, or urgency, prompting screen readers to alter pitch or volume to indicate emphasis. In contrast, `<b>` simply applies visual bold styling without conveying any added semantic weight to search engines or screen readers.

why_wrong.0: Neither tag alters font color by default; both render in bold black text unless styled with CSS.

questions.question: Explain why using `!important` to solve this issue is a poor architectural practice, and provide two clean, maintainable engineering solutions to resolve the styling conflict.
marking_points: Identifies why `!important` is harmful: Breaks the natural cascade, escalates 'specificity wars', and forces subsequent overrides to also require `!important`.

Solution 1 (Refactor base styles): Remove the ID selector `#confirm-drop` from the base stylesheet and restyle using utility classes (e.g., `.btn { background-color: green; } .btn.btn-danger { background-color: red; }`).

Solution 2 (Specificity matching/chaining): Target the element using an ID-qualified selector (e.g., `#confirm-drop.btn-danger` or `button#confirm-drop`) which achieves specificity (0,1,1,0), cleanly overriding the base ID rule.
States the principle of keeping CSS specificity flat for enterprise maintainability.
questions.answer:
1. Why `!important` is an Anti-Pattern:
Appending `!important` breaks the natural cascading flow of CSS. It creates technical debt by initiating a 'specificity arms race'—any future theme changes or modal dialogs targeting this button will also be forced to use `!important`, making the codebase brittle and unmaintainable.

2. Two Clean Engineering Solutions:
- Solution 1: Refactor Base Styles to Classes (Best Practice): Remove the ID selector from the CSS entirely. IDs should be reserved for JavaScript DOM access and in-page anchor links, not styling hooks. Re-author the base style as a class `.btn` and state modifier `.btn-danger`. Because both are classes, source order allows `.btn-danger` to win naturally:
```css
.btn { background-color: green; }
.btn-danger { background-color: red; }
```
- Solution 2: Chain Selector to Match Specificity (Quick Fix): If the base ID cannot be edited immediately, chain the class to the ID in the override selector: `#confirm-drop.btn-danger { background-color: red; }`. This gives a specificity score of (0,1,1,0) (score 110), which cleanly defeats the base ID selector (0,1,0,0) (score 100) without resorting to `!important`.
questions.explanation: Disciplined frontend engineering keeps specificity low and avoids `!important` hacks.

Provides a robust system font stack with multi-word quoting and generic fallback (e.g., `font-family: -apple-system, BlinkMacSystemFont, 'Segoe UI', Roboto, Helvetica, Arial, sans-serif;`).
Explains why font stacks must terminate in generic `sans-serif` or `serif`.

questions.question: What is the purpose of the `<label for="xyz">` element?
questions.answer: It binds a text label to an input with `id="xyz"`. It enhances accessibility for screen readers and allows users to click the text label to focus or toggle the input control.
questions.explanation: The '<label for="element-id">' element provides a programmatic association between a descriptive text label and a form control. questions.question: What is the key difference between `readonly` and `disabled` on form inputs during submission?
questions.answer: A `readonly` field cannot be modified by the user, but its value IS submitted to the server. A `disabled` field is grayed out and its value is NOT submitted to the server.
questions.explanation: The fundamental difference between form control states: A 'readonly' input prevents user editing but its value IS submitted with the form payload during submission. A 'disabled' input is greyed out, cannot be focused or modified, and its value is strictly EXCLUDED from the submitted form data payload. (W3C HTML5 Form Submission).

questions.question: Why should `<a href="..." target="_blank">` always be paired with `rel="noopener noreferrer"`?
questions.answer: For security: without it, the newly opened external page can access your page's JavaScript execution context via `window.opener` and redirect your users to a malicious phishing site (known as reverse tabnabbing).
questions.explanation: When opening links in a new tab via 'target="_blank"', modern web security requires adding 'rel="noopener noreferrer"'. Without 'noopener', the target page gains access to the originating window's 'window.opener' object, enabling malicious reverse tabnabbing phishing attacks. (MDN Web Security; OWASP Foundation).
